videos.title: The Jazz Trumpeter Behind Neo-Soul's Greatest Era
videos.description:
Even if you don't recognize his name, you've heard his sound. Jazz trumpeter Roy Hargrove played trumpet on, and contributed arrangements to, D'Angelo's Voodoo, Common's Like Water for Chocolate, and Erykah Badu's Mama's Gun. He was equally at home with neo-soul and hip-hop, and straight-ahead acoustic jazz. At the same time he was contributing to era-defining Soulquarian projects, he was producing music with his jazz quintet.

Today, jazz pianists Adam Maness and Peter Martin listen to his 2008 masterpiece Earfood and explore why it may be the perfect jazz album for the jazz-curious neo-soul fan.

videos.title: Jazz pianists still hear something new in Black Messiah, 12 years later
videos.description:
D'Angelo's Black Messiah is one of the greatest albums of the 21st century. You can hear his musical influences all over it: Prince's arrangements, the Bee Gees' falsettos, Jimi Hendrix's guitar, Sly's groove. But the alchemy that makes Black Messiah so powerful could only come from one mind: D'Angelo, the artist who gave us Voodoo and Brown Sugar.

Jazz pianists Adam Maness and Peter Martin unpack D'Angelo and the Vanguard's Black Messiah track by track, detailing what their trained ears hear in the music, and highlighting new textures, harmonies, and song structures you may have missed on the first listen. 

Plus, Peter shares stories about his friendship and working relationship with legendary trumpet player Roy Hargrove.

Featuring Bill Evans on piano, Scott LaFaro on bass and Paul Motian on drums, this 1962 live album has become the template for every AI jazz playlist. And yet, it stands apart as one of the greatest jazz piano trio albums of all time. Pianists Adam Maness and Peter Martin listen to the full album, track-by-track, describing what they hear in the music that lends this album its undeniable humanity.

videos.description:

So we're upping the stakes ... with a draft. Adam and Peter each present their top tracks from Songs in the Key of Life, compare and contrast, and see who comes out on top with the best lineup.

videos.title: Kind of Blue Isn't Perfect. It's Better
videos.description:
Miles Davis's Kind of Blue is one of the greatest albums of all time - possibly THE greatest. But it's not perfect. 

In this special episode of You'll Hear It, jazz pianists Peter Martin and Adam Maness break down this classic record, track-by-track, to uncover why it has become so legendary. They dig into what's really going on in the music during this album's best moments: Miles's trumpet solo on "So What", Wynton Kelly's piano solo on "Freddie Freeloader", John Coltrane's entrance on "Blue in Green".

Plus - we learn more about what Miles was doing in his early years, his break from bebop, what he thought of Bill Evans's approach, and the production and engineering techniques that give Kind of Blue its unique sound.

Miles Davis was born just outside of St. Louis 100 years ago this week. To celebrate his centennial birthday, Adam and Peter filmed this episode in front of a live audience at The Sheldon Concert Hall in St. Louis, MO.

videos.title: The Two Days That MADE Miles
videos.description:
Cookin', Relaxin', Workin', and Steamin' capture Miles Davis on one of music history's most remarkable upswings. He had recently become clean after a years-long heroin addiction that led to his exclusion from major record labels and clubs. And now, in 1956, he had a deal with Columbia - the Cadillac of record labels - and a band he loved: Red Garland on piano, Philly Joe Jones on drums, Paul Chambers on bass and John Coltrane playing the sax. 

In this episode of You'll Hear It, jazz pianists Peter Martin and Adam Maness go through each album. They discuss the outsized influence of Ahmad Jamal, Red Garland's Red spread technique, the power of Miles's chatter on Relaxin' and whether this is the greatest rhythm section in the history of recorded music. 

Whether this is your first introduction to Miles Davis, or you've been listening to these albums for years, you'll walk away from this episode with a new understanding of, and appreciation for, Miles and his first great quintet.

videos.title: The Album Marvin DIDN'T Write Might Be His Best Work
videos.description:
Marvin Gaye's I Want You could be one of his greatest albums, and he didn't even write it. Producer Leon Ware wrote most of the songs for himself. Marvin Gaye was only supposed to record the title track. But he heard Leon playing a demo of the album one night and stayed up listening until morning. The next day, he asked Ware if he could have the whole thing.

In this episode, Peter and Adam break down why the title track, "I Want You", might be one of his best songs, and whether the rest of the album can possibly live up to it.

This episode was recorded before the passing of James Gadson (June 17, 1939 – April 2, 2026), the drummer on I Want You. Gadson was one of the defining session drummers of 1970s soul. He was the drummer behind "Lean On Me," "I Will Survive," "Express Yourself", and the groove that powers this very album. Rest in peace, James.

videos.title: The Accidental Album that Became a Global Phenomenon
videos.description:
Buena Vista Social Club: The album so good it's life-affirming. And it almost didn't happen.

In 1996, an American musician landed in Cuba to record a music project with Malian musicians. But when they didn't show up, Ry Cooder and his producer, Juan de Marcos González, went looking for replacements. 

That's when they found Compay Segundo, Ibrahim Ferrer and Rubén González, who had seen their musical prime decades earlier in the 40s and 50s. Compay was nearing his 90s, and some believed he had died, until he showed up on Buena Vista Social Club. Rubén hadn't played in years, and didn't even own a piano. 

But together with a cast of all-star Cuban musicians, they created what would become the best-selling world music album of all time. 

How did Buena Vista Social Club become a global phenomenon? 

In this episode of You'll Hear It, Peter Martin and Adam Maness listen to the record track-by-track to understand what makes this album so magnetic, and how it holds up 30 years later. Plus - a FIRST in You'll Hear It history.

videos.title: How Fela Kuti Turned Music Into a Weapon - DUAL SCREEN AUTO SYNC
videos.description:
This is a Dual Screen Experience! You'll need to watch this on a TV or Computer and also have your phone - otherwise this video won't make much sense. 

Use your phone to head to https://sync.diggingthegreats.com/watch/fela-kuti-companion-video to automatically sync the accompanying video. Full explanation in the video above - let me know how you enjoyed this format! 

Note: there are strategically placed YouTube ads in between each section of this video and you'll need to hit stop on your phone during an ad break, and then just hit play to resync again once the video continues. If you have YouTube Premium, you DO NOT need to stop your phone at any point. 

This is a re-release of the Fela Kuti video that automatically syncs the companion video. To watch the manual sync video, click here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TqTn-aS9W04

If you don’t know who Fela Kuti is, I’m about to introduce you to your new favorite artist. If you’re familiar with him already, you know he invented a new genre of music called Afrobeat, combining funk, jazz, and West African rhythms, but that’s only half of the story. The other half is what his music stood for. Today we’re diving into the music and world of Fela Kuti, and we’ll see how he created some of the best music ever made, gave hope to people for generations, and nearly toppled a dictatorship.

Thanks to Jad Abumrad for chatting with me. Go check out his podcast "Fela Kuti: Fear No Man" wherever you listen to podcasts! https://podcasts.ap

videos.title: Vince Staple’s *BRILLIANT* Kobe Bryant Scheme Breakdown
The Most GENIUS Number Bars in Rap History
videos.description:
From Rakim to Kendrick Lamar, this is the story of hip-hop’s obsession with numbers.

In this episode of Dissect, host Cole Cuchna breaks down the evolution of “number bars” - a lyrical tradition where rappers use math, numeric sequences, and wordplay to showcase technical skill and encode hidden meaning.

Beginning with Rakim’s groundbreaking verse on “My Melody” (1986) - a quatrain built around groups of seven that secretly mirrors his own 21-letter name - we trace how MCs have used numbers as both a mathematical signature and a symbolic device for decades. From Melle Mel’s divine 7-count in “Superrappin” to Jay-Z’s “22 Twos”, Biggie’s “Ten Crack Commandments,” and Mos Def’s “Mathematics,” numbers became an essential part of hip hop tradition and lyricism.

By the 2000s, artists like Lupe Fiasco, J. Cole, JID, Vince Staples, and Kendrick Lamar transformed number schemes into complex storytelling tools. We unpack everything from Lupe’s hidden 3–2–1 countdown on Kanye West’s “Touch the Sky” to Kendrick’s quantum-level equations on “Nosetalgia.”

Three of the Bhavishyavani Future Soundz founders – Ashim Ahluwalia, Mukul Deora and Tejas Mangeshkar – share stories of how they mixed foreign and local inspirations together, and the uphill battles of trying to establish a new culture of nightlife in a country undergoing its own cultural and demographic explosion.

#BhavishyavaniFutureSoundz #DanceGrooves #RedBullMusicAcademy
__________________________

As electronic dance music and rave culture washed over America and England in the ’90s, India still moved to a more traditional nightlife beat that included Goa trance and chart-approved hits. Indian nightlife began to change at the turn of the century when small groups of artists and creatives across the country found ways to showcase the music and aesthetics they’d witnessed abroad. In Mumbai, it was the Bhavishyavani Future Soundz collective who helped kickstart the evolution of the city’s club culture. 

A multimedia collective composed of amateur DJs, film and design professionals, Bhavishyavani Future Soundz threw their first party on May 13, 1999. Over the years visual themes like traditional Indian weddings or politics would mix with sets of jungle, dub techno and live performances by then-upcoming Indian electronic acts such as MIDIval Punditz. Singer and multimedia artist Lina Pereira found a vessel for expression via the alias of Linn Da Quebrada. Emerging from the favelas of São Paulo in 2015, Pereira took inspiration from her friend Lineker, who fronts the soul band Liniker E Os Caramelows, and merged early experience in theater with baile funk. The result has been a blistering sound and presence that aims to confront established notions of race, gender and sexuality by speaking directly to the political embedded in everyday life and actions. In 2018, Linn Da Quebrada released her debut album _Pajubá_ and starred in the documentary _Bixa Travesty_, both of which explore her background, the search for love and the desire to kill the man inside of her in order to be free.

videos.description:

The DJ behind Portugal's tribal house scene shares stories of Lisbon’s early club culture, how DJs and venues had to operate within existing cultural constrictions and just how Lisbon’s tribal sound made the jump over the Atlantic. 

You can read more on DJ Vibe here...
► https://www.redbullmusicacademy.com/lectures/dj-vibe

#DJVibe #Housemusic #RedBullMusicAcademy

When Yury Chernavsky began work as a music producer in late ’70s USSR, there was little around him to draw inspiration from and so he looked to the advances and innovations happening in the West. His career began in the late ’60s as a jazz musician, playing the violin and saxophone as a member of various orchestras, including ensembles led by Russian jazz stars Oleg Lundstrem and Leonid Utyosov as well as Muslim Magomayev’s State Jazz Orchestra of Azerbaijan. Inspired by Coltrane, Count Basie and Quincy Jones, Chernavsky worked the concert circuit for over a decade before moving into musical direction, composition and production. In the ’80s he emerged as one of Russia’s first modern-day music producers, working with rock and pop groups as well as experimenting with early synthesizer and studio technologies. Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis are one of the greatest songwriting and producing duo in music history. Meeting on the same ’70s Minneapolis music scene that produced Prince, the pair formed the band Flyte Time, an outfit that would morph into the original line up of one of the most storied funk groups of the era, the Time. By 1983 the duo had begun more actively pursuing songwriting and producing, commencing a series of essential R&B singles for the likes of the S.O.S Band, Cherrelle, Cheryl Lynn, Alexander O’Neal and others. In 1986 they began their now-legendary association with Janet Jackson, producing the Grammy Award-winning LP _Control_, the first of many career-defining efforts over the next three decades. In addition, they have crafted classics for the likes of Force M.D.’s, Sounds of Blackness, New Edition, Human League, George Michael, Usher, and Mary J. Blige.

__________________________

Drummer, vocalist and serial collaborator Yoshimi Yokata AKA YoshimiO has been an inescapable presence in the Japanese and international experimental rock and avant-garde scene for over 30 years. Hailing from Okayama, YoshimiO began her career in 1986 with the band U.F.O or Die, a side project of experimental vocalist Yamatsuka Eye, before joining Eye’s Boredoms a year later and eventually becoming one of its longest serving members. 

She began releasing music under the name Yoshimi P-We (now YoshimiO) in 1993, all the while collaborating across various projects – the experimental ensemble OOIOO, the Saicobab quartet, which fuses Indian raga traditions with punk and electronic music – and with international musicians including Kim Gordon, Mats Gustafsson, Susie Ibarra and Robert Lowe. While best known as a drummer and vocalist, Yokata also plays the trumpet and keyboard and often works in improvisational contexts.

The one constant across his expansive output is weight: a weight of volume, of bass, of emotion. It's an approach and a philosophy that’s informed just as much by punk as it is by the legendary London soundsystems of Jah Shaka and Aba Shanti-I.

From creating drones in Ableton to using a metal spring as a bass and a metal sheet as percussion, FM Einheit shows how to tap into the freedom of music as a language. 

Named after the abbreviation for the frequency modulation of shortwave radios he used when he first began making music, Einheit immersed himself in the post-punk world of late ’70s Germany before joining Einstürzende Neubauten in the early ’80s as a percussionist. During his time with the influential West Berlin band, Einheit built custom-made instruments, often using metal, and used hammer drills to create new sounds. Live performances would in turn feature dramatic use of the instruments with banging and destruction, which cemented the band’s uncompromising image and set Einheit on his own unique creative path, writing and performing music with unconventional instruments and approaches. Yuzo Koshiro is a Japanese composer, arranger, and programmer whose contributions helped change video game music. Having discovered video games and their music at an early age, Koshiro learnt to program using an NEC PC-8801 before landing his first jobs in the industry in early 1980s Tokyo, scoring the background music for games like Bosconian, Tower of Druaga and Sega’s 1987 hit Shinobi. 
Breaking away from the conventions of early BGM soundtracks, which favored pop, rock and jazz, Koshiro setup his own company, Ancient, and quickly established himself as a pioneer in the field thanks to his programming knowledge and early mastery of FM sound chips.

In the second half of the 2010s, the Toronto-raised native of Jamaica further expanded his reach with the global hits “Work” for Rihanna and “Controlla” for Drake, as well as collaborations with Kendrick Lamar, PARTYNEXTDOOR and Lana Del Rey.

videos.title: Ken Swift of The Rock Steady Crew Breaks Down Breaking & More (Audio Only) | The Almanac of Rap
videos.description:
Before breaking became a global industry, and long before it became an Olympic event, Ken Swift was helping define what the dance could be. A longtime Rock Steady Crew member and one of the form’s most important second-generation B-boys, Swift joins Donwill on The Almanac of Rap to revisit the late-’70s and early-’80s New York scene where DJs, concrete floors, gymnasiums and neighborhood crews turned movement into a new language. He explains why “breakdancing” was always a media invention, how Rock Steady expanded across boroughs, and why early breaking was as much about character, rhythm and community as athleticism.

Swift also looks back on the films that exported breaking to the world (from Wild Style and Beat Street to the now-iconic Flashdance sequence) and weighs what happens when an underground culture becomes a global institution. He talks candidly about breaking’s Olympic debut, why he chose to watch and judge it from home, and why the future of the form depends less on spectacle than on education, tradition and teaching young dancers how to exist inside the culture, not just battle inside it. Ken Swift breaks down:

- How Rock Steady Crew’s second generation came together across the Bronx and Manhattan.
- Why “breakdancing” was never the language the culture used for itself.
- What Beat Street, Wild Style and Flashdance got right (and wrong) about early hip-hop.
- How he really felt about breaking becoming an Olympic sport
- Why education and cultural memory matter

videos.title: From Digable Planets to Harvard: Ladybug Mecca's Next Chapter (Audio Only) | The Almanac of Rap
videos.description:
The Digable Planets icon on Blowout Comb, her Harvard fellowship, and tracing hip-hop's Afro-Brazilian roots.

Before Digable Planets helped redefine the sound of alternative hip-hop, Ladybug Mecca was a young artist absorbing Brazilian music, jazz, and the rhythms of her family's home. Three decades after Blowout Comb became a cornerstone of jazz-inflected hip-hop, the pioneering MC joins Donwill to discuss her latest chapter as a recipient of Harvard University's Nasir Jones Hip-Hop Fellowship. Her research traces the connections between hip-hop and Afro-Brazilian traditions, from Candomblé drumming to capoeira, challenging the idea that hip-hop simply arrived in Brazil rather than finding a culture already connected through rhythm, movement, and shared African ancestry.

Ladybug Mecca reflects on her Brazilian parents, the influence of MC Lyte and Queen Latifah, and the enduring relevance of Digable Planets' Blowout Comb. She opens up about navigating hip-hop as a young woman, her friendships with Guru and Bahamadia, her collaborations with Prince Paul and Brookzill!, and why documenting Black creativity is increasingly urgent in an era of cultural erasure. Still an avid music discoverer, Mecca also shares her excitement for a new generation of women MCs and explains why her next creative chapter is as much about recovering history as making it. Ladybug Mecca breaks down:

- How the Nasir Jones Hip-Hop Fellowship is helping her investigate connections between Afro-Brazilia

videos.title: Jon B on '90s R&B, Babyface, & the Hip-Hop Records That Shaped Him (Audio Only) | The Almanac of Rap

Before Jon B. became one of the defining voices of '90s R&B, he was a kid surrounded by records, instruments, and a family of classically trained musicians. In this episode of the Almanac of Rap, the singer, songwriter, and producer traces his journey from teaching himself piano and drums to meeting Babyface and Tracey Edmonds, signing his first record deal, and releasing his debut album Bonafide. What began as a dream of becoming a behind-the-scenes songwriter and producer evolved into a recording career after Babyface encouraged him to step into the spotlight. Jon B breaks down:

- Inside the Native Tongues and Soulquarians orbit: Visiting Q-Tip's studio, learning MPC techniques from J Dilla, and receiving encouragement from the artists who inspired him.

videos.title: Saul Williams on Leap Life, the Politics of Art & the Power of Poetry | The Almanac of Rap
videos.description:
What happens when an artist refuses to separate creativity from revolution? Poet, musician, actor, filmmaker, and cultural provocateur Saul Williams joins Donwill for an expansive conversation about Leap Life, his first solo studio album in seven years, and Songs My Mother Taught Me, a new nonfiction book examining the experiences and ideas that shaped his political consciousness. 

Working alongside producer Carlos Niño, Williams transforms experimental soundscapes, dance rhythms, and ancestral memory into music that confronts artificial intelligence, colonialism, and the machinery of modern power. From recording a track inside Cairo's bustling streets on his leap-day birthday to hosting listening séances honoring the lives lost to violence, Williams reveals why his latest work is both deeply personal and unapologetically political.

Saul travels with Donwill back to the Brooklyn poetry scene of the 1990s, where Williams shared open-mic stages with future cultural luminaries, including Yasiin Bey and Erykah Badu, before becoming a defining voice of the spoken-word movement. Saul breaks down:

- The making of Leap Life: How Carlos Niño helped transform years of experimental demos into a cohesive album.
- The ideas behind Songs My Mother Taught Me, the influence of Paul Robeson and W.E.B. Du Bois, and why Williams believes music should challenge power rather than reinforce it.

Digable Planets helped redefine the possibilities of hip-hop in the early 1990s, blending jazz, funk, political consciousness, and a distinctly cosmic sensibility into a sound that resisted easy categorization. They reflect on the success of Reachin' (A New Refutation of Time and Space), the complicated cultural politics of winning a Grammy in hip-hop's early years, and how their revolutionary upbringing informed the music and visual identity of Blowout Comb. videos.title: Maiya the Don Talks "Precious Cargo" & Shifting From Beauty Content to Music | The Almanac of Rap
videos.description:
Maiya the Don spent three years figuring out what she actually wanted to say. After Hot Commodity introduced a Brooklyn rapper capable of moving between drill, pop and straight-up bars, touring with Flo Milli and building an audience that first knew her as a beauty creator, Maiya found herself confronting a harder question: what does her music sound like when she's no longer trying to prove she can do everything? 

On this episode of The Almanac of Rap, she talks to Donwill about creating The Fine Print Club, her book club built around reading, community and creating space for Black women; recommends everything from S.A. Cosby to DMX; and hilariously puts her literary knowledge to the test against some of urban fiction's wildest book titles. 

Between books and bars, she also makes a case for independence, explains why artists shouldn't run from being content creators and delivers a warning to anyone tempted to underestimate her pen: Precious Cargo (her new album) may be personal, but Maiya the Don still came to rap. Maiya the Don breaks down:

- Why Precious Cargo became the coming-of-age album she needed three years to make
- Turning a beauty-content following into the foundation for a rap career
- Why independence gives her control over both her artistry and narrative
- Building The Fine Print Club and creating literary community for Black women
- Why “TSA” is her answer to anyone questioning a woman rapper's pen

Marsalis and the Masters was captured live during the opening concerts of Jazz at Lincoln Center’s 2025-26 season, which is dedicated to Marsalis’ enormous contributions both to the institution and to the music itself. videos.title: Joe Block – There Is Always Hope
videos.description:
Pianist, composer, and bandleader Joe Block has spent his career refining his distinct musical voice, collaborating with icons like Wynton Marsalis, Kurt Rosenwinkel, and Gary Bartz as well as serving as associate music director for George Clooney’s Good Night, and Good Luck on Broadway. The Steinway Artist and 2027 American Piano Awards finalist steps out front with There Is Always Hope, his new album released by Blue Engine Records. The record marks not only Block’s debut as a bandleader but his first album built entirely of his own compositions: it’s the culmination of seven years of writing and musical collaboration.

The record features special guest Kurt Rosenwinkel and a battle-tested ensemble consisting of trumpeter Noah Halpern; saxophonists Chris Lewis, Morgan Guerin, Dylan Band, and Abdias Armenteros; bassist Samuel Harris; and drummer Christian McGhee. The group’s collective sound has served as Block’s compositional laboratory since 2019, and their telekinetic connection results in a bold, cathartic statement, taking listeners on a journey through dynamic emotional landscapes anchored by a shared sense of joy and optimism.

Listen now at https://www.jazz.org/block!

“Composing and performing alongside Plexus No. 27 was a truly unique experience. I felt its thousands of threads as an extension of my harp strings, a space where color, sound, and music became one. “There’s something about Kerry James Marshall’s figuration of the Black body that feels like abstraction, and that is the site in which I can find myself. It’s where the music can communicate with the piece, and it’s where the painting can become a score. “Our Town” invites us to listen through the image. I wanted to widen the view of the painting with a sound that added another vantage point.”

videos.title: BRIDGES: Mary Halvorson + Tomas Fujiwara / In Exaltation of Flowers
videos.description:
BRIDGES
Episode 4
Mary Halvorson and Tomas Fujiwara performing in front of "In Exaltation of Flowers" by Edward Steichen

"This was an entirely unique artistic experience. Being surrounded by In Exaltation of Flowers by Edward Steichen was quite intense: from a larger perspective, we found ourselves wrapped in massive panels saturated with beauty and color, and then zooming in on the small details of each character, we found humor, darkness and breadth. Our improvisation sought to mirror the relationship between the big picture and the minutia, as well as the elegant contrast between shadow and light.

The process was both inspiring and fun, and the resulting film is completely different from any of our other creative work. We are grateful to be a part of this series, and send big thanks to the talented, engaged, and kind crew we worked with."

 – Tomas Fujiwara and Mary Halvorson

videos.title: BRIDGES: Ambrose Akinmusire / Marie Bannerot McInerney
videos.description:
BRIDGES
Episode 3
Ambrose Akinmusire performing in front of "Trace Me Back" by Marie Bannerot McInerney 
Bill Reiter: Sound Collaborator and Producer

"The title, Trace Me Back, made me think about my first experience with creative improvised music: seeing the Art Ensemble of Chicago at the original Yoshi’s. At the same time, the material in the piece reminded me of that white lab coat Lester Bowie wore. The title and the material were both taking me back in time, just in different ways.

The hanging forms started to feel like marks on a chronological graph. Each one held a different stretch of time, a different era or version of myself. As I moved back and forth through the space, I was moving through my influences, experiences with my heroes, and lessons learned. I was moving through my own timeline at different speeds, without trying to make the history too clean. The drone underneath is the ancestors.

There’s also folding (origami). Not just as a visual form, but as something people do to fit within what society has decided is acceptable for them. People marginalized by race, gender, sexuality, class, disability, or age are constantly asked to adjust themselves. It happens creatively too. You begin reshaping the work, or reshaping yourself, so you can be understood, accepted, or simply allowed into the room. At some point, that adjustment can become a kind of self-erasure. You may fit, but you may also be failing some part of yourself in the process. I’m thinking about t

videos.title: BRIDGES: Joel Ross / Lenore Tawney
videos.description:
BRIDGES
Episode 2
Joel Ross performing in front of In Fields of Light by Lenore Tawney

"When I first encountered In Fields Of Light, I was struck by the sheer size of the tapestry and the way light reflected off of it. I couldn't help but think how appropriate the title felt, as if I were actually standing in a field of light. Seeing the work inspired me to use a continuous rhythmic figure between my hands while remaining within a single tonal space. The simplicity and focus of the work compelled me to meditate on one idea and explore its journey.

I'd like to thank my wife, Laura Bibbs; my team, Bryan Farina, Chris Mees, and Gift Pratoomvieng; Jazz at Lincoln Center; and the Crystal Bridges Museum for making this happen." - Joel Ross

videos.title: BRIDGES: Elena Pinderhughes / Julie Mehretu
videos.description:
BRIDGES
Episode 1
Elena Pinderhughes performing in front of Retopistics: A Renegade Excavation by Julie Mehretu

"When I play, I always try to ground myself in a story I’m trying to tell. Playing with Julie Mehretu’s artwork right there in front of me, I felt it come alive in a whole new way, like the painting and I were each telling a piece of the same story. I felt connected to her work. The closer I looked at her canvas, the more it broke open into smaller moments and layers, each one holding its own little story. So, the piece is built with the base layers telling the first story and then I improvised my own story on top of them. I loved the chance to bring the two worlds together." 
–Elena Pinderhughes

videos.title: Alumni Spotlight: Lilly Clark
videos.description:
This Month's Alumni Spotlight is on Lilly Clark, a Senior Software Engineer at SpaceX, and part of the inaugural Jazz at Lincoln Center Youth Orchestra program in the 2013-14, now part of Jazz Academy. As a student, Lilly spent her Saturdays taking the Staten Island Ferry to Manhattan to rehearse with the orchestra at Jazz at Lincoln Center.  One standout memory: when her saxophone malfunctioned during rehearsal, Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra member Sherman Irby generously lent her his instrument, a moment of mentorship she’ll never forget. Though Lilly didn’t pursue music professionally, the principles she learned through jazz, especially improvisation,  continue to shape her work. She credits the music with teaching her to think on her feet, trust her preparation, and adapt in real time.

Are you a JALC alumni? Sign up to be part of the network at jazz.org/alumni

videos.title: Streaming Now: WE THE PEOPLE, by the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra with Wynton Marsalis
videos.description:
Stream the full album now at jazz.org/people

Blue Engine Records is proud to announce the release of We the People, the latest album from the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra with Wynton Marsalis. Recorded live in 2019, this suite of music emerged from an historic collaboration between Jazz at Lincoln Center and the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art that united two great American institutions in service of using our shared cultural heritage to lead the way toward a better future.

The project began when the JLCO’s masterful composers were asked to select a single work of art from Crystal Bridges’ incomparable collection as inspiration for a new original work. The resulting songs, stitched together into a suite, present a stunning big band portrait of our nation’s history, scoring works from acclaimed artists such as Romare Bearden, Thomas Cole, Stuart Davis, and Grace Hartigan. Both stirring and elegiac, We the People celebrates America’s unparalleled cultural contributions to the world; and by bringing together Jazz at Lincoln Center and Crystal Bridges, the record shows how the arts can connect disparate communities and unite us all.

videos.title: Attend Jazz at Lincoln Center's Summer Jazz Academy!
videos.description:
Jazz at Lincoln Center’s Summer Jazz Academy is a premier two-week residential program for 48 of the nation’s most advanced high school jazz musicians and vocalists (grades 9–12). Led by a distinguished faculty, the SJA offers intensive training through big bands, small combos, private lessons, and classes in aesthetics, culture, history, performance practice, and pedagogy. Students are admitted by audition and will present multiple public performances alongside members of the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra at Bard College and Jazz at Lincoln Center in summer 2026.

Learn more at https://jazz.org/jazz-academy/

videos.title: Endea Owens Explores the Spirit of Africa in a New Premiere
videos.description:
Member of The Late Show with Stephen Colbert band, bassist Endea Owens premieres a new work February 20-21 inspired by the spirit of Africa, drawing on the history of Black Americans and Duke Ellington's Cotton Club, featuring dance performance by Sekou McMiller + Friends.

Join trumpeter Jeremy Pelt and bassist Endea Owens for a powerful evening of newly commissioned works featuring vocalists, dancers, and full ensembles, set in the breathtaking, sky-high Appel Room. Inspired by the music and spirit of Africa, these performances offer bold, contemporary perspectives on Africa’s enduring influence on jazz, brought to life through voice, rhythm, and movement.

videos.title: Jeremy Pelt on Afro-futurism and the Mysticism of Masks
videos.description:
Trumpeter Jeremy Pelt explores Afro-futurism and the mysticism of masks in a powerful new work premiering February 20–21 in the Appel Room. Watch as he discusses the ideas and inspirations shaping the music.

Join trumpeter Jeremy Pelt and bassist Endea Owens for a powerful evening of newly commissioned works featuring vocalists, dancers, and full ensembles, set in the breathtaking, sky-high Appel Room. Inspired by the music and spirit of Africa, these performances offer bold, contemporary perspectives on Africa’s enduring influence on jazz, brought to life through voice, rhythm, and movement, and featuring a special guest appearance by dance company Sekou McMiller + Friends.

videos.title: Fredara Hadley on Afrobeat to Afrobeats
videos.description:
Juilliard ethnomusicologist Fredara Hadley explores the origins and evolution of Afrobeat and Afrobeats, examining their global impact and deep connections to jazz. Her insights set the stage for Big Band Afrobeat to Afrobeats, Jazz at Lincoln Center’s upcoming performance on March 6–7 in the Appel Room.

Tickets: https://jazz.org/concert/big-band-afrobeat-to-afrobeats-ulysses-owens-jr-with-michael-olatuja/?utm_source=youtube+interview&utm_id=youtube+interview

videos.title: Alumni Spotlight: Joe Block
videos.description:
In 2016, pianist and composer Joe Block was selected as the Essentially Ellington Dr. J. Douglas White Student Composition/Arranging Contest winner. That year, his piece “Volcanic Suite” was selected by saxophonist Ted Nash and recorded and performed by the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra with Wynton Marsalis. Following EE, Block participated in two years of JALC's Summer Jazz Academy and went on to graduate from the Columbia–Juilliard dual-degree program in music. Now an in-demand professional, he leads the Future of Jazz Orchestra, has written for the JLCO, toured internationally, subbed on piano with the JLCO, and most recently performed as a jazz pianist in George Clooney’s Good Night, and Good Luck on Broadway. This spring, he will release a new album on Blue Engine Records.


Are you a JALC Alumni? Join the network at https://jazz.org/alumni

videos.title: Marilyn Maye – No Bad News (from "The Magic of Marilyn Maye: Live at Jazz at Lincoln Center")
videos.description:
The Magic of Marilyn Maye: Live at Jazz at Lincoln Center spotlights some of the legendary vocalist’s best moments on Jazz at Lincoln Center’s stages over the past decade. A favorite of Ella Fitzgerald’s and Johnny Carson’s, Maye has been enchanting audiences for an extraordinary eight decades through her boundless energy, pristine delivery, and witty interpretations of the American Songbook. Dubbed the “Queen of Cabaret,” “Medley Maye,” and “Super Singer,” Maye’s artistry shines anew on her first release in years, which stands as a joyful testament to her unerring superpower: making listeners feel.

Listen to the album now: jazz.org/marilyn

videos.title: Chris Lewis and Alexa Tarantino collaborate on Duke in Africa
videos.description:
Duke in Africa is a powerful tribute to Duke Ellington’s profound connection to the African continent. Staged nearly 60 years after Ellington's historic performance in Senegal, this concert explores how the legendary composer’s works drew inspiration from African rhythms and cultural themes. Co-music directors, the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra’s own Chris Lewis and Alexa Tarantino, lead the JLCO in a dynamic program featuring selections from Ellington’s works. Watch them discuss their process in an exclusive behind-the-scenes look.

Get tickets: jazz.org

videos.title: Look Inside Jazz at Lincoln Center's JAZZ ACADEMY
Alumni Spotlight: Paul Brown
videos.description:
Paul Brown is an adjunct lecturer at Borough of Manhattan Community College and an alumnus of Essentially Ellington, having competed with Newark Academy. In high school, jazz was his team sport. Like any great team, his school’s jazz ensemble, Chameleon, worked collaboratively year after year toward selection for Essentially Ellington, dedicating countless hours to preparation, performance, and excellence. The ensemble shared the pride of a job well done and drew inspiration from their “coach” and band director, Julius Tolentino.

In this month’s Alumni Spotlight, Paul reflects on his Essentially Ellington experience, his enduring appreciation for jazz, and the surprising connections between jazz and chemistry.

Are you a JALC Alumni? Join the network at https://jazz.org/alumni

videos.title: Afropop Worldwide Living Room Session #4 | Razia
videos.description:
We are happy to share Living Room Session #4, part of Afropop’s series of live performances recorded in living rooms, homes and music studios around New York City.
On a warm summer morning, Malagasy-born singer and songwriter Razia Said welcomed us into her Harlem apartment for an intimate and uplifting set.
A longtime New Yorker, Razia writes and sings mostly in Malagasy, drawing on the rhythms, melodies and instruments she grew up with to address environmental destruction in Madagascar, resilience and homecoming. 

For this session, Razia takes us through songs from different moments in her career, including the albums Akory (2015) and The Road (2018). The opening track, “Zanako,” from Akory, means “my child” in Malagasy and looks toward the children of Madagascar as the country’s future. “Mbola Velogno, ” written for her latest album, The Road, means “still alive.” The song carries the same unshakable sense of hope that sits at the heart of much of Razia’s work.

videos.title: Afropop Living Room Sessions: Kotoko Brass and Mohammed Alidu
videos.description:
For this second Afropop Living Room Session, Kotoko Brass is joined by Ghanaian musician Mohammed Alidu, who sings and performs on the lunga talking drum, a traditional instrument of northern Ghana. 

Kotoko Brass brings together the traditional drumming of central Ghana, Caribbean rhythm section grooves, and the bright horn energy of New Orleans to create what the Boston Globe has called “propulsive, infectious party music.” 

The band was founded by brothers Ben and Brian Paulding and includes master Ghanaian percussionists Attah Poku and Kwame Ofori alongside a seasoned rhythm and horn section. 

The collaboration brings together musical traditions from different regions of Ghana in a performance grounded in rhythm, dance, and collective celebration.

videos.title: Afropop Living Room Sessions: Aba Diop & the Yermande Family
videos.description:
We are proud to introduce the first edition of the Afropop Worldwide Living Room Sessions. This edition features Aba Diop and the Yermande Family, a band that blends Senegalese traditions--Wolof, Mande and more--in a thrilling ensemble presentation. The band was formed in Dakar, Senegal, but now has a second home in the U.S. This session was recorded amid the band's tour to promote their 2025 album, Family.  

Aba Diop is a master of the sabar drum, the beating heart of Senegal’s most popular dance music: mbalax. The percussive center of the Yermande Family is Diop’s fiery duo volleys with tama player Samba Ndokh, a veteran of Cheikh Lo’s band. Noumoukunda Cissoko on kora brings the Mande music element to the band, while griot vocalist Zeyna Ngom Diop delivers commanding lead vocals, often joined by Aba Diop and Samba Ndokh. Guitarist Jason Hosier, the one American in the band, has spent significant time learning guitar styles in Senegal, and it shows.

This is a band that can command every inch of a concert stage, with kinetic moves, dramatic dancing and irresistible ambiance. Here we find them in the at-home setting, seated, at ease and relaxed, but no less electrifying.

videos.title: Pedrito Martinez Rocks the Afropop Hall of Fame Induction!
videos.description:
Dive into the enthralling world of Afropop as we celebrate the prodigious Pedrito Martinez on his monumental achievement of receiving the Afropop Hall of Fame Award. This prestigious accolade is a testament to Martinez's unparalleled musicianship and indelible mark on the global music arena. Witness the euphoric moments from the award ceremony and concert that left everyone in awe and revel in the musical genius of Pedrito Martinez. The electric atmosphere was a homage to the rhythmic heritage that Martinez so impeccably embodies. Subscribe to our channel for more captivating musical journeys and groundbreaking achievements by stalwarts of the African diaspora. 

Read more: https://afropop.org/articles/a-night-with-pedrito-mart%C3%ADnez-at-drom.

videos.title: Mokoomba’s Unforgettable Return to London
videos.description:
Mokoomba’s Unforgettable Return to London
After 6 years since the legendary Mokoomba last played in London, they finally made their very special appearance at the Jazz Cafe, in Camden Town. And there is no better place to perform than this brilliant, intimate venue. Three words to describe this musical experience would be playful, entertaining, and healing. It might be one of the most unique and enjoyable live events the Jazz Cafe has seen. It appeared the crowd had already anticipated this, as the audience began streaming an eager hour and a half before the scheduled start time to secure themselves a prime spot in the crowd. Read Hannah Allchurch´s review here. https://afropop.org/articles/mokoombas-unforgettable-return-to-london

videos.title: Daymé Arocena  Para mover los pies Visualizer & Lyrics 4K
Howard Armstrong speaks with Banning Eyre in Boston: 1:11/2000
videos.description:
In January 2000, having survived Y2K, Afropop Worldwide's Banning Eyre met American music legend Howard Armstrong (1909-2003) in his apartment in Boston, where he was living at age 92 with his companion and fellow musician Barbara Ward. The goal was to tape an interview of Howard's remembrances of his Black string music heritage stretching back to his father's late 19th century youth. The talk went long, far more than could fit in the APWW episode The African American String Music Tradition, encored for Black History Month 2023. 
This is an audio edit of their conversation that day.

videos.title: M’Bembé (my ancestors) the new video/single from Natu Camara drops January, 9. 2023.
videos.description:
M’Bembé (my ancestors) the new video/single from Natu Camara drops today. 

In her latest video/single M’Bembé, singer songwriter Natu Camara calls for national unity and cohesion in her home country Guinea. 

The video is produced in partnership with a branch of the UN (UNDP) and was officially launched in Conakry on January 9th. The press conference was attended by journalists, and representatives of radio and television stations.

Under a full moon and the suggestive branches of a tree, Natu is joined by a group of young female musicians who perform a powerful anthem in the name of the ancestors for harmony and peace.

videos.title: Interview/New Music: Savannah V "talks about it" with Tejano Nation as her new single drops today
videos.description:
"Talk About It," a hip hop song in English that features heavy rapping and tough-talking lyrics, proves the impressive versatility of longtime Tejano artist Savannah V's voice as she tackles a style unlike any she's done before.

The story behind the song, which features rapper, Squishy, evolved from a surprising five little, but powerful, words that one female artist, diva, you could say, spoke against a fellow diva, whom she dismissed with: "I don't even know her."

Watch the interview here, or, for the complete package, visit TejanoNation.net to read the article and watch the masterfully done music video for "Talk About It," available today on all digital streaming platforms.

#talkaboutit #savannahv

videos.title: EXCLUSIVE INTERVIEW: Meet new artist Heather Jolene Alcantar
videos.description:
Meet San Angelo native Heather Jolene Alcantar, an aspiring Tejano artist whose first single release, "No Me Vayas a Dejar," flows fresh and flirty as a pop cumbia brimming with feel-good vibes and a reggae beat.

Alcantar chose to share her personal and powerful story with Tejano Nation first. 

And, while she did not choose the historic role she finds herself in as Tejano music's first transgender artist, this courageous and upbeat singer does not take the role, or the responsibility that comes with it, lightly.

videos.title: Michael Salgado Interview with Lilymarie
Interview: La Machy and Savannah V dare to swear w/premiere of collab, "CHATUM"
videos.description: This collaboration sparked interest from the start as both La Machy and Savannah V exude power, strength, and an edginess that makes people take notice. But, "CHATUM," the fourth single from La Machy, as a solo artist, featuring Savannah V, also an award-winning vocalist, will make many take notice. For many reasons. The language, yes, but more importantly, viewers will hear emotive voices and see passionate portrayals from two female artists you can't ignore. The two stars speak exclusively with Tejano Nation about the story behind "CHATUM," which stands for something you say when no other words will do. A few might say, "No, they didn't!" But most will sing along as they relate with the story behind the song.

videos.title: Interview: Stevie D gets real with Tejano Nation
videos.description: In an exclusive interview with Tejano Nation, Freddie Records artist and Tejano Music Award winner Stevie D shares the personal and devastating struggle that he battled for more than a year.  His perseverance and determination helped him persevere, and now, the popular and charismatic vocalist said he is both focused and ready to face the challenges that await him. And, he's highly motivated to please fans again with his distinctive voice and suave style.

videos.title: INTERVIEW: Stefani Montiel - Mis Favoritas, Vol. 2 (Ballads)
videos.description:
Popular, longtime Tejano artist Stefani Montiel talks to Tejano Nation about the six songs on her recently-released Vol. 2 of her EP series, "Mis Favoritas." Montiel, a versatile vocalist, re-creates the experiences of six classic and timeless Tejano ballads that evoke special memories in her life and career. Known for her energetic stage performances and danceable cumbias, Montiel celebrates an exciting career that spans three decades. 

The songs featured on "Mis Favoritas, Vol. 2 (EP)," include: "Si Quieres Verme Llorar," "Que Casualidad," "No Te Olvidare," "Entre Las Sombras," "Me Estoy Enamorando," and "Borracho de Besos."

videos.title: Interview: Nathan Acosta talks debut single, getting his break
videos.description: Talented, genuine, and gifted, accordionist/vocalist Nathan Acosta, 18, just released his debut single, "Solo," on the Freddie Records label with the worldwide release set for April 19, 2024. The mostly self-taught musician sits down with Tejano Nation to talk about how he got his start, what it's like to work and perform alongside two of Tejano music's most popular artists, Jesse Turner of Grupo Siggno, and Jennifer Pena, La Princesa de la Musica Tejana, and, recalls what happened exactly one year ago today that changed his life.

videos.title: Interview: Jaime DeAnda - Debut Solo Album, 'Volando Solo,' and new label NextGen Latinx Records
videos.description:
A trailblazer and trendsetter for the accordion sound and style, veteran Tejano/Conjunto artist Jaime DeAnda has captivated audiences for more than four decades with his master accordion skills, distinctive vocals, and high-energy dance moves. In 2018, after more than 30 years together, DeAnda and Los Chamacos, known as the premier conjunto showband, split in a move that shocked fans. 

However, DeAnda continued his journey as a solo artist, most recently, joining forces with a new label, NextGen Latinx Records, and releasing his first solo album, aptly titled, "Volando Solo". The much-awaited album will be available on all digital streaming platforms on April 5, 2024.  But fans can buy it now in either digital format so they get it immediately or order online at either nextgenlatinx.com or jaimedeanda.com and get it delivered.

DeAnda and NextGen Latinx Records CEO Mike Torres III talk with Tejano Nation about the new album, exciting future projects in the works for DeAnda's musical career, and even address his split from Los Chamacos, and his goal to always entertain his fans whether through his recordings or live performances.

videos.title: Teaser: Gary Hobbs Interview with Tejano Nation
videos.description:
See a few of the many highlights from our interesting and revealing talk as the longtime Tejano artist and fan favorite Gary Hobbs openly talks with Tejano Nation about everything from his latest single on Freddie Records, "Llegaste a Mi Corazon," written by Freddie Martinez, Sr., to his musical inspirations including Bruno Mars, yes, I said, Bruno Mars.

The smooth-voiced Hobbs,, of Eagle Pass,  boasts 40 years in the industry, and proved to be both an enjoyable and refreshingly candid  artist to interview. He is a unique mix of old-school Tejano  who promotes traditional values such as discipline yet he can easily talk about new Latin and pop artists like Karol G and Bruno Mars. And, he'll be on TikTok soon!

Don't miss the full interview and story, coming soon on  Tejano Nation

Hobbs is currently promoting his Latin Grammy nominated album, "Sin Fin."
Fans can catch Hobbs on social media, his podcast, and live at this year's Tejano Music Awards Fan Fair!!

videos.title: Pete Astudillo Interview - 022824
videos.description:
Tejano vocalist, award-winning songwriter, and energetic performer Pete Astudillo sits down with Tejano Nation to talk about his role in Tejano music history and his recent return to recording with a deeply personal song that will surely resonate within the Latino community. 

With humble and hard-working beginnings in the border town of Laredo, Texas, Astudillo recalls his struggles for recognition at the start of his music career, the once-in-a-lifetime opportunity  that let his talents shine as a singer, dancer, and composer with the iconic Selena y Los Dinos, and his own hit-producing solo career. Astudillo held a unique, front-row perspective as a member of Tejano music's most famous band led by the genre's brightest star.

videos.title: Playing with Chick Corea | Stanley Clarke on The Questlove Show
videos.description:
Philly's own Stanley Clarke, one of the bassists who plugged in and moved the instrument to the front of the stage, finally joins Questlove to retrace his career. He looks back on growing up in Philadelphia, his strict classical training at Settlement Music School and the day Chick Corea talked him out of joining the orchestra to start Return to Forever. Stanley also tells the story behind his 1-of-1 Alembic bass, explains why Larry Graham is the most important electric bassist ever and remembers his close friendship with Jaco Pastorius.                                                                                                                        

Then come the wild stories: touring with Keith Richards and Ronnie Wood in the New Barbarians, recording with Aretha Franklin and getting a songwriting credit from Paul McCartney. He also explains how a Pee-wee's Playhouse gig grew into a film-scoring career, including the Boyz n the Hood screaming saxophone cue that's suddenly viral 35 years later. It's a deep look at courage, freedom and making music that changes minds. 

Stanley Clarke's new box set, Last Train to Sanity [https://lasttraintosanity.com/], is available now.

videos.title: Iconic Songs About the End | Lenny Kaye on The Questlove Show
videos.description:

Questlove and Lenny nerd out as fellow record obsessives, swapping stories about organizing vinyl, seeing Jimi Hendrix twice, meeting Patti Smith (whom he played bass for ever since), and recording “Piss Factory” in the final 15 minutes of a session at Electric Lady. Lenny also talks about his new solo debut, Goin' Local [https://lennykaye.lnk.to/GoinLocal], out now on Yep Roc. Made for artistic closure, not to chase a trend, the personal, unhurried record came from a simple conviction: “because I’m my favorite artist.” He reflects on creativity, his enduring love of music, and the crates he’s digging through now.

videos.title: Luther Vandross Covering Superstar | Nat Adderley Jr on The Questlove Show
videos.description:
For Nat Adderley Jr., serving as Luther Vandross’ musical director and longtime pianist was one chapter in a remarkable musical life—and a partnership that helped shape the sound of modern R&B. In conversation with Questlove, Nat looks back on making “Never Too Much,” flying in from Houston to play “A House Is Not a Home,” and trying to talk Luther out of recording the Carpenters’ version of “Superstar.” As Vandross is inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, Nat recalls the grandeur of Luther’s stage shows and the loss of drummer Yogi
Horton. He also reflects on how his arrangement of “If This World Were Mine” found new life in Kendrick Lamar’s “Luther.”

The funny, unpredictable conversation also touches on Nat’s new album, Took So Long [https://linktr.ee/natadderleyjr]—his first as a leader and a return to the Jazz roots that run through his family and his work. In a personal full-circle moment, Quest' tells Nat how a
protest song Nat recorded at 15 with his uncle Cannonball Adderley changed his life.

videos.title: Infinity Song in Central Park
videos.description:
The Questlove Show welcomes Infinity Song's Abraham, Angel, and Israel Boyd. The Detroit-born siblings spent years busking at Central Park's Bethesda Fountain before signing with Roc Nation and earning the support of some of music and film's biggest stars.

The three Boyds talk about being homeschooled by a mom who handed out sour gummy candy watches as rewards for grammar drills, learning harmony as section leaders in their dad's choir, and moving to New York in 2006 out of necessity rather than in pursuit of a dream. Infinity Song also discusses rebuilding the band after founding member Victory went solo, and how going viral with ""Haters Anthem"" motivated the quartet (including sister Momo) to set their sights on even bigger accomplishments.

Along the way, there are plenty of surprises: meeting Oprah and Jon Batiste while busking, stories about 2000s-era Motor City, and more.

videos.title: Nat Adderley, Jr. On Growing Up In A Famous Household | Questlove Show #shorts
videos.description:
For Nat Adderley Jr., serving as Luther Vandross’ musical director and longtime pianist was one chapter in a remarkable musical life—and a partnership that helped shape the sound of modern R&B. In conversation with Questlove, Nat looks back on making “Never Too Much,” flying in from Houston to play “A House Is Not a Home,” and trying to talk Luther out of recording the Carpenters’ version of “Superstar.” As Vandross is inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, Nat recalls the grandeur of Luther’s stage shows and the loss of drummer Yogi
Horton. He also reflects on how his arrangement of “If This World Were Mine” found new life in Kendrick Lamar’s “Luther.”

The funny, unpredictable conversation also touches on Nat’s new album, Took So Long [https://linktr.ee/natadderleyjr]—his first as a leader and a return to the Jazz roots that run through his family and his work. In a personal full-circle moment, Quest' tells Nat how a
protest song Nat recorded at 15 with his uncle Cannonball Adderley changed his life.

videos.title: Chuck D | The Questlove Show
videos.description:
In one of the most requested and long-awaited conversations in this show’s history, Chuck D finally joins Questlove in the studio. What unfolds is an intimate conversation about the art, science, and spirit behind Public Enemy—especially during the group’s formative years.

Chuck traces the spark from hearing James Brown's "Blow Your Head" at roller rinks to the Frankenstein tape loops that gave birth to "Public Enemy No. 1," "Rebel Without a Pause," and "Bring the Noise." He recalls writing classic verses on the move, reflects on his early jobs, and breaks down the record-collecting discipline that fueled the Bomb Squad's dense sonic collages.

Along the way, Chuck opens up about aging as an MC, meeting James Brown, and Flavor Flav's evolution. This is Hip-Hop history, music nerdery, and deeply human storytelling from one of Rap's most important and enduring voices.

Chuck D and past QLS guest John Densmore of The Doors have teamed up as do+pe for a new collaborative album, No Country For Old Men [https://bio.to/nocountryforoldmen]. The latest issue of Chuck's Rap Central Station [https://www.silverbackpublishing.rocks/rap-central-station-shop/] publication is available now.

videos.title: Lenny Kaye & Questlove discuss Bob Dylan & More
videos.description:
Before the Ramones and the Sex Pistols, Lenny Kaye was clerking at Village Oldies on Bleecker Street. In 1972, he compiled Nuggets—and its liner notes helped shape the emerging idea of Punk Rock.

Questlove and Lenny nerd out as fellow record obsessives, swapping stories about organizing vinyl, seeing Jimi Hendrix twice, meeting Patti Smith (whom he played bass for ever since), and recording “Piss Factory” in the final 15 minutes of a session at Electric Lady. Lenny also talks about his new solo debut, Goin' Local [https://lennykaye.lnk.to/GoinLocal], out now on Yep Roc. Made for artistic closure, not to chase a trend, the personal, unhurried record came from a simple conviction: “because I’m my favorite artist.” He reflects on creativity, his enduring love of music, and the crates he’s digging through now.

videos.title: John Carpenter's View on Filmmaking After a Long Career In It | The Questlove Show
videos.description:
Questlove sat down with director and composer John Carpenter in Hollywood to discuss Cathedral, a graphic novel [https://stormkingcomics.com/] and Heavy Metal album [https://johncarpentermusic.bandcamp.com/album/cathedral] inspired by a single dream. Carpenter tells how a bongo lesson from his father led to the iconic Halloween theme. He also talks about casting Kurt Russell after their Elvis TV movie, why The Thing was his hardest shoot, and says The Exorcist remains the scariest movie ever made.

Along the way, Carpenter turns the tables and interviews Questlove, sparking a lively debate about The Beatles and whether music has reached “creative diminished returns.” It’s a funny, engaging conversation between two directors who work in different worlds but share a love of making music.

videos.title: Live Performance: Should it Sound Like the Record? | Nat Adderley Jr.
videos.description:
For Nat Adderley Jr., serving as Luther Vandross’ musical director and longtime pianist was one chapter in a remarkable musical life—and a partnership that helped shape the sound of modern R&B. In conversation with Questlove, Nat looks back on making “Never Too Much,” flying in from Houston to play “A House Is Not a Home,” and trying to talk Luther out of recording the Carpenters’ version of “Superstar.” As Vandross is inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, Nat recalls the grandeur of Luther’s stage shows and the loss of drummer Yogi
Horton. He also reflects on how his arrangement of “If This World Were Mine” found new life in Kendrick Lamar’s “Luther.”

The funny, unpredictable conversation also touches on Nat’s new album, Took So Long [https://linktr.ee/natadderleyjr]—his first as a leader and a return to the Jazz roots that run through his family and his work. In a personal full-circle moment, Quest' tells Nat how a
protest song Nat recorded at 15 with his uncle Cannonball Adderley changed his life.

videos.title: Richard Smallwood – "Hebrews 11" (Rare Original Demo) | From the Personal Archive
videos.description:
In 2014, I had the extraordinary privilege of spending a week with the legendary Richard Smallwood while producing The Richard Smallwood Singers Documentary at his request. During that time, Richard invited me into his creative world and played this early demo of what would eventually become part of his Hebrews 11 live recording. I was so captivated by it that I asked if I could have a copy, and he graciously shared it with me.

Years later, while revisiting my personal archives, I rediscovered this recording and was immediately reminded of the brilliance I witnessed firsthand. Today, I'm honored to share this rare glimpse into the creative process of one of the most prolific composers, arrangers, and musicians in the history of Gospel music. My hope is that it not only preserves a small piece of Richard's extraordinary legacy but also offers inspiration to future generations of musicians, worshippers, and lovers of Gospel music.

videos.title: Viva Tejano | Trailer
videos.description:
Latin music is ascending in the U.S., and, in some surprising ways, much of the story behind the trend begins in Texas. On Viva Tejano, host J.B. Sauceda talks with legendary tejano artists and well-known tejano music fans about how the music has shaped their lives. It’s a nostalgic journey and a close look at the influences behind many of today’s biggest acts in música Mexicana.

Audio subscribers to Texas Monthly can listen to episodes one week early, and get access to exclusive bonus material. Visit texasmonthly.com/audio (https://texasmonthly.com/audio)  to learn more.
